_meta: A single task whose duration is measured while the wall clock is corrected backward mid-run, used to show that you must measure an elapsed interval with a monotonic clock, not the wall clock. The wall clock (time.time, the calendar clock) answers 'what time is it' and is periodically re-synced to an external reference: an NTP daemon steps it, a manual set changes it, a DST fall-back rewinds it. Any of these can move it backward, so the difference of two wall-clock readings is not the real elapsed time -- and when a backward step lands inside the interval you are timing, the measured duration is too small or even negative, which then poisons rate limits, timeouts, retry backoff, and profiling. A monotonic clock (time.monotonic, perf_counter) answers 'how much time has passed' and is guaranteed never to go backward; its absolute value is meaningless (it counts from an arbitrary origin) but the difference of two readings is always the true elapsed interval. true_intervals are the real seconds that pass between consecutive readings (real time only moves forward, so these are all positive); wall_jumps are corrections applied to the wall clock just before each reading (a negative value is a backward step, e.g. an NTP correction); wall_start and mono_start are the two clocks' arbitrary origins. From these the two clocks' readings, and the duration of the task measured each way, are computed: the monotonic measurement equals the sum of the true intervals, while the wall measurement is off by the jumps that land inside the interval.
